newsitem.title: USA: White House, Congress seem on brink of budget deal.
newsitem.headline: White House, Congress seem on brink of budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and the Republican-led Congress on Friday were on the brink of a landmark deal to balance the budget for the first time since 1969 as negotiators sought to iron out last-minute glitches.

Administration and congressional officials said the deal involved major spending cuts, as well as tax reductions, in the drive to balance the budget by 2002, but that there were still unresolved issues.
Clinton, a Democrat, planned to telephone top legislators in Congress to work out the latest wrinkles in the budget talks, said an official close to the negotiations.

"We're still not there yet. We've still got some work to do," said the official, who asked not to be identified. "Clinton plans to make some additional calls to the Hill to review certain elements that are still in dispute."
Clinton delayed his departure for an afternoon meeting with Senate Democrats in Baltimore in order to get a briefing on the talks from his chief of staff, Erskine Bowles.

"Things are at a delicate stage. We are still ironing out some problems," Sen. Frank Lautenberg, a Democrat from New Jersey, told reporters on Capitol Hill as he shuttled between the offices of top legislators.

But legislators on both sides were also hinting that an agreement involving about $85 billion in tax cuts over five years along with spending cuts in a variety of government programmes was on the verge of being wrapped up.
"If you are thinking of going to the beach today, I would delay it for a little," said Representative John Kasich, the Ohio Republican who chairs the House of Representatives Budget Committee.

As described by officials, the deal under discussion would cut spending across the government over five years, notably in the Medicare and Medicaid health care programmes, and offer $85 billion in tax cuts to benefit investors and families.
Clinton said earlier he was optimistic on chances for a deal but suggested taxes remain a bone of contention.

"We have to be very careful not to set conditions in motion which could explode the deficit again because of the way the tax cut is written or other provisions are written after this budget period ends," he said.

Chief of Staff Bowles and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin went to Capitol Hill on Friday morning to resume negotiations, with Bowles suggesting that progress had been made on the tax cut issues, which he called "minor."

A House of Representatives Republican source said a White House request for additional spending was blocking progress. "If this thing falls apart, it's because the White House wants more spending," the source said, declining to be named.

If the White House and the congressional Republicans come to an agreement among themselves, the other difficult problem they will face will be to sell the pact to their own parties, both of which have factions who oppose the outlined agreement.
The proposed deal's $85 billion tax cut over five years was expected to include reductions in capital gains and estate taxes and a $500 child tax credit, officials said.
Much of the government's five-year savings would come from the Medicare health care programme for the elderly. Its spending would fall by $115 billion through 2002.

Savings of over $20 billion would come from the Medicaid health care programme for the poor. Other domestic programmes would be cut $68 billion and defence by about $80 billion from the amount that would be spent under current policies.
However, Clinton would receive $32 billion in spending for his education, environment and other new initiatives.
The Democratic White House and Republican Congress have been at loggerheads over the budget since Republicans won majority control of both U.S. legislative chambers in 1994.
The two sides failed to reach a balanced budget agreement over the ensuing two years, leading to two partial shut-downs of the federal government in late 1995 and early 1996.
